screening_decisions.reason: Basic science laboratory study examining drug effects on Na+ channels expressed in mammalian cells. Not a clinical RCT comparing phenobarbitone vs phenytoin monotherapy in patients with epilepsy.
Prospective observational cohort study of 525 patients with newly diagnosed epilepsy. Not a randomised controlled trial comparing phenobarbitone vs phenytoin monotherapy.

Double-blind study comparing multiple anticonvulsants including phenobarbital and diphenylhydantoin (phenytoin) in patients with focal brain damage and epilepsy. May contain relevant comparative data for phenobarbitone vs phenytoin monotherapy. Uncertain enough to warrant full-text review.
Cochrane Review protocol about congenital malformations from AED exposure during pregnancy. Not a primary RCT comparing phenobarbitone vs phenytoin monotherapy for seizure control.
Review article discussing principles and practice of AED use. Not a randomised controlled trial.
Epidemiological survey estimating prevalence/incidence of neurologic disorders. Not a randomised controlled trial comparing antiepileptic drugs.

Randomised controlled trial comparing phenobarbital vs phenytoin monotherapy in 94 children aged 2-18 years with partial and generalised tonic-clonic epilepsy. Directly meets all selection criteria: RCT design, compares the two drugs of interest, appropriate population and seizure types.
Methodology paper describing techniques for extracting summary statistics for meta-analyses. Not a clinical trial.
Meta-analytic study estimating global burden of epilepsy. Not a randomised controlled trial comparing antiepileptic drugs.
Randomised controlled trial comparing phenobarbital vs carbamazepine (not phenytoin) in children with epilepsy. Does not meet criteria as it does not compare phenobarbitone vs phenytoin.
Prospective observational study examining congenital malformations in children exposed in utero to phenytoin and carbamazepine. Not an RCT comparing monotherapy efficacy for seizure control.
Population-based registration study describing natural history of epileptic seizures. Not a randomised controlled trial.
Incidence study of epilepsy in HMO populations. Not a randomised controlled trial comparing antiepileptic drugs.
Review article summarizing literature on AED effects on behavior and cognition in children. Not a primary randomised controlled trial.
Book chapter describing methods for assessing risk of bias in systematic reviews. Not a clinical trial.
Prospective observational registry study examining malformation risks from AED exposure during pregnancy. Not an RCT comparing phenobarbitone vs phenytoin monotherapy for seizure control.
Review article discussing epidemiology and diagnostic challenges in epilepsy. Not a randomised controlled trial.
Review article about phenytoin uses in dermatology and side effects. Not a randomised controlled trial comparing monotherapy for epilepsy.
Basic science study examining GABA receptor modulation by carbamazepine and phenytoin in cell cultures. Not a clinical randomised controlled trial.
Animal study examining phenytoin-folate interactions in rats. Not a clinical randomised controlled trial in humans with epilepsy.

This is a prospective community-based cohort study, not a randomised controlled trial. It does not compare phenobarbitone versus phenytoin monotherapy; instead it examines prognostic factors for epilepsy remission.

This is a randomised controlled trial where patients were randomly assigned to monotherapy with phenytoin (18 patients) or phenobarbitone (18 patients) or carbamazepine. While the primary outcome is cognitive effects, it is an RCT comparing the drugs of interest as monotherapy in epilepsy patients.
This study evaluates combination therapy (carbamazepine combined with phenytoin and/or phenobarbital), not monotherapy. The selection criteria specifically require monotherapy comparisons.

This is a 10-center, double-blind randomised controlled trial comparing monotherapy with phenobarbital and phenytoin (among other drugs) in adults with partial and secondarily generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Meets all selection criteria.
This is a methodological paper describing statistical methods for meta-analysis, not a primary randomised controlled trial comparing antiepileptic drugs.

This is a randomised, double-blind clinical trial comparing monotherapy with phenobarbitone and phenytoin (plus valproate) in 151 children with generalized tonic-clonic convulsions aged 4-12 years. Each child received one active drug and 2 placebo tablets. Meets selection criteria.
This is a methodological paper examining outcome reporting bias in systematic reviews, not a primary randomised controlled trial comparing antiepileptic drugs.
This is a methodological paper discussing equivalence trial design principles, not a primary randomised controlled trial comparing antiepileptic drugs.
This is a population-based observational incidence study, not a randomised controlled trial. It does not compare any antiepileptic drug treatments.
Based on the title, this is a methodological paper about measuring inconsistency in meta-analyses, not a primary randomised controlled trial comparing antiepileptic drugs.
This is a reporting guideline paper (PRISMA statement), not a primary randomised controlled trial comparing antiepileptic drugs.
This is a review article describing mechanisms of action of antiepileptic drugs, not a primary randomised controlled trial.

This is a prospective randomised pragmatic trial comparing monotherapy with phenobarbitone and phenytoin (plus carbamazepine and valproate) in 243 adult patients (16+ years) with tonic-clonic or partial with/without secondary generalised seizures. Meets all selection criteria.

This is a randomised double-blind, triple crossover study comparing phenobarbital and phenytoin (plus carbamazepine) in 15 patients with partial complex epilepsy. While the primary outcome is cognitive effects, it is an RCT comparing the drugs of interest as monotherapy. Included conservatively for potential data extraction.

This is a controlled trial focused on evaluating carbamazepine (Tegretol). While it may mention comparisons to other drugs, the primary focus is not comparing phenobarbitone versus phenytoin monotherapy.
This is a position paper on epilepsy classification terminology, not a primary randomised controlled trial comparing antiepileptic drugs.
This is a network meta-analysis/systematic review, not a primary randomised controlled trial. The selection criteria require primary RCTs.
This is a multiple treatment comparison/network meta-analysis synthesizing data from 20 randomised trials, not a primary randomised controlled trial itself.

This is a controlled prospective study evaluating carbamazepine in patients whose seizures were not controlled by current medications. The focus is on carbamazepine, not comparing phenobarbitone versus phenytoin monotherapy.
This is a Cochrane systematic review about antiepileptic drugs in pregnancy and neurodevelopmental outcomes, not a primary randomised controlled trial.

This is a basic science laboratory study investigating the mechanism of action of diphenylhydantoin (phenytoin) and carbamazepine on sodium channels in mouse neuroblastoma cells. It is NOT a randomised controlled trial involving human patients with epilepsy. The study uses patch voltage clamp procedures on cell cultures, which does not meet the requirement for clinical RCTs comparing monotherapy in people with focal onset or generalised onset tonic-clonic seizures.

This is an epidemiological observational study reporting incidence rates of epilepsy and unprovoked seizures in a population from 1935-1984. It is NOT a randomised controlled trial and does not compare any interventions or treatments. The study describes disease occurrence patterns rather than evaluating treatment efficacy, so it does not meet the selection criteria for RCTs comparing phenobarbitone versus phenytoin monotherapy.

This is a methodological paper discussing the advantages and challenges of individual patient data (IPD) meta-analysis in anti-epileptic drug research. While it references randomized monotherapy trials, this publication itself is NOT a primary randomised controlled trial. It is a secondary analysis/methodology paper describing how IPD meta-analyses can be conducted, not an original RCT comparing phenobarbitone versus phenytoin monotherapy.

This is a basic science preclinical study investigating the molecular mechanism of barbiturate action (pentobarbitone and phenobarbitone) on GABAA receptors in cultured rat hippocampal neurons. It uses whole-cell voltage clamp and single channel recording techniques on animal cell cultures. This is NOT a randomised controlled trial involving human patients with epilepsy, and does not evaluate clinical outcomes of monotherapy treatment. Therefore it does not meet the selection criteria.

This IS a randomised controlled trial that meets the selection criteria. It is a prospective, randomised, pragmatic trial comparing four antiepileptic drugs used as monotherapy in children with newly diagnosed epilepsy. The study includes both phenobarbitone and phenytoin as treatment arms, allowing for direct comparison between these two drugs. The population consists of children aged 3-16 years who had at least two previously untreated tonic-clonic or partial seizures (with or without secondary generalisation), which matches the required seizure types (focal onset seizures or generalised onset tonic-clonic seizures). Outcomes include time to first seizure and time to achieving 1-year remission, which are relevant clinical endpoints for this review.
